extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in US media, politics, and media-ethics controversies
extracted.subtask_description: A news article summarizing and evaluating allegations that a prominent TV host exaggerated or fabricated wartime reporting; contrasts contemporaneous reporting, eyewitness accounts, and the subject's later statements. Focuses on media-ethics and factual accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must withstand scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: “don't withstand scrutiny—even claiming he acted heroically in a war zone that he apparently never set foot in.” (quote from Mother Jones describing O’Reilly's wartime claims)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article uses Mother Jones’ investigation as the standard: public claims about having 'experienced combat' should be verifiable against records, contemporaneous reporting, and eyewitness testimony. Examples from the piece contrast O’Reilly’s boasts with the absence of corroborating evidence in his book and contemporary news coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate representation of physical presence in conflict zones
rubrics_metrics.description: O'Reilly has said he was in a 'war zone' in the Falklands and 'covered the Falklands war' but also denied ever saying he was on the Falkland Islands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists and commentators should clearly distinguish whether they were physically on battlefields/islands versus covering events from nearby countries (e.g., Argentina/Uruguay). The piece highlights contradictions between O’Reilly’s TV/book wording and his later denials as an evaluative concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration with contemporaneous reports and colleagues' accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Mother Jones compared O’Reilly’s accounts with news reports from the time and statements from other journalists (e.g., Bob Schieffer, Susan Zirinsky, Robert Fox) who say 'Nobody from CBS got to the Falklands' and that accredited journalists on the islands were mostly British.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims about wartime reporting should align with contemporaneous newsroom records, footage, and testimony from other reporters who covered the event; discrepancies undermine credibility. The article uses multiple named sources to check O’Reilly’s account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate civil unrest/protests with combat
rubrics_metrics.description: “The protest in Buenos Aires was not combat. Nor was it part of the Falklands war. It happened more than a thousand miles from the war—after the fighting was over.” (Mother Jones' critique)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting should avoid labeling distant protests or post-war unrest as 'combat' or 'war zone' experiences. The piece criticizes O’Reilly for calling a Buenos Aires protest 'combat' when contemporaneous reports show minimal violence and no connection to fighting on the islands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid invoking unverified combat credentials to bolster policy positions
rubrics_metrics.description: O’Reilly often cites his combat credentials in order to refute the arguments of people who do not agree with his views on foreign policy, e.g. challenging a retired colonel with the claim he had 'a hostile point an M-16 at your head from 10 yards away.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using asserted personal combat experience as rhetorical authority in debates on military policy requires that those experiences be accurate and verifiable; otherwise it is misleading. The article treats such rhetorical use as a reason to scrutinize the subject's claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between memoirs/books and factual record
rubrics_metrics.description: In his 2001 book The No Spin Zone O’Reilly writes 'I've reported on the ground in active war zones from El Salvador to the Falklands,' yet Mother Jones notes 'nowhere in the book does O'Reilly mention experiencing any combat during the Falklands war.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal memoirs and published accounts should reflect factual experiences; absence of specific claims in an earlier memoir can be used to evaluate later, more dramatic public statements. The article contrasts book text with later anecdotes as a test of accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects should respond to inquiries from investigators/publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: Although O’Reilly reportedly didn’t respond to calls for comment from Mother Jones, other figures (e.g., Susan Zirinsky) did provide statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When allegations arise, responding to requests for comment is a professional expectation; failure to engage makes verification harder and shapes public assessment. The article notes O’Reilly’s reported lack of response as relevant to evaluating the dispute.
